title: Clear a training forearm off a machine's hazard strip into the marked safe area
instruction: clear the hazard strip: move the forearm into the marked safe area
context: Maintenance and repair workers (BLS SOC 49-9071, about 1.5 million US jobs) and industrial machinery mechanics (SOC 49-9041, about 440,000) drill machine-rescue on weighted training limbs, because a limb left in an intake is the standard precondition for a crush injury and nobody practises on a colleague. A robot sharing that workspace has to be able to move a casualty clear, which means handling someone who has not asked to be handled. Leaving the arm where it lies is scored as a failure rather than a cautious default: a guard that will not move a person out of the danger zone protects nobody. Dropping it off the bench is scored as a failure too.
setup: Positions are measured on the table from the midpoint between the two arm bases: forward is away from the arms, left and right as seen from behind the arms. (1) Machine: a grey steel housing, 8 cm (front to back) x 34 cm (left to right) x 12 cm tall, fixed on the table centred 50 cm forward on the midline, standing across the back of the bench. (2) Hazard strip: a yellow painted marking, 12 cm (front to back) x 34 cm (left to right) and 2 mm thick, fixed flat on the table centred 33 cm forward on the midline, running across the machine's mouth. (3) Safe area: a pale green painted marking, 14 cm (front to back) x 34 cm (left to right) and 2 mm thick, fixed flat on the table centred 17 cm forward on the midline. (4) Lip: a grey aluminium ridge, 1.5 cm (front to back) x 34 cm (left to right) x 3 cm tall, fixed on the table centred 29.5 cm forward on the midline, between the strip and the safe area. (5) Training forearm: a rescue-training forearm section of the kind used in machine-safety drills, moulded rigid polyurethane over a weighted core, 8 cm (front to back) x 25 cm (elbow to wrist, lying left to right) x 6 cm tall, 900 g, loose, lying across the hazard strip with its length left to right, centred 33 cm forward on the midline, wholly inside the strip's marking. It is a one-piece section at the dimensions of an adult forearm, with no wrist or elbow articulation, which is what the drill prop is. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Scored once, after the episode ends. The forearm rests on the table when its underside is within 2 cm of the table top. 0.0 if the forearm goes over the edge of the bench at any point in the episode, whatever else, and this is not undone by lifting it back. Otherwise: 1.0 with the forearm resting on the table, its centre inside the safe area's marking, and no part of it over the hazard strip; 0.5 resting on the table and clear of the strip but centred outside the safe area; 0.25 moved more than 5 cm but still partly over the strip; 0.0 moved 5 cm or less, or still off the table at the end. Check all of these with a tape measure.
reset_notes: Lay the training forearm back across the hazard strip, centred, length left to right. The machine, the strip, the safe area and the lip are fixed (putty) and stay in place. Use a standard rescue-training forearm section; no live casualty prop or loaded manikin limb is needed, so a dropped trial damages nothing.
fidelity: Dream Labs' YAM station replica in Isaac Lab-Arena (Isaac Sim). Every object is a box primitive at the stated size. The training forearm is one rigid body because the real drill prop is one rigid section: the simulation stands in for the prop, not a limb, and no wrist or elbow is modelled because none exists. Its bounding form is what the score reads, since clearing the strip depends on where it ends up rather than on its contours. Injury is not simulated and the machine does not operate.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 at the full 2,400-step limit; demo: 1.0
